summary: This unit teaches you to book clients into a salon or spa and to check them out at the end of their visit. You will learn to take a booking with the right details, allow the right time with a worker who has the skills, fit in skin tests and consultations, handle cancellations, late arrivals and no-shows, and avoid double booking. At check-out you will prepare an accurate bill with discounts, deposits and GCT, take payment, offer rebooking, aftercare and home-care products, update the record and say goodbye.

blocks.p: A salon's appointment book is its plan for the day. Every service, every worker and every client's time is in it. Book well, and the day runs smoothly: clients are seen on time, workers are busy but not rushed, and the salon earns what it can. Book badly, and the day falls apart: double bookings, long waits, idle chairs and lost money. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees and covers both ends of a visit: the **booking** that starts it and the **check-out** that ends it.

Both ends need the same three things: **accuracy** (the right details, the right time, the right sum), **knowledge** of the salon's services, prices, workers and policies, and **courtesy**, because booking and paying are the two moments when a client decides whether to come back.

blocks.h: A visit from first call to goodbye

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays, including time and money sums) and two group practical tasks. In the first you take phone bookings for a day at a salon and spa from a blank appointment page: ordinary bookings, a colour that needs a skin test, a client asking for a worker without the skills, a cancellation and waiting list, a moved booking and a bridal group with a deposit. In the second you check out clients with a product sale, a discount voucher, a deposit, a complaint and a rebooking, with GCT at the rate the assessor gives.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Greeting and directing clients when they arrive belongs to another unit. This one is about the booking before the visit and the desk at the end of it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Every salon needs **one** system that everyone uses. It may be a paper appointment book or a computer or online booking system. The danger is having two: a book at the desk and a stylist's own notebook, or a computer and a paper diary that do not match. Then two clients turn up for one chair.

blocks.h: How the page is laid out

blocks.p: A day's page has a **column for each worker** and a row for each time slot, usually every 15 minutes. A booking is written in the worker's column, across all the rows its service needs. A glance at the page then shows who is busy, who is free and when. Breaks, lunch, days off, training and days when a worker is off sick are **blocked out** in the column, so that nobody is booked into them.

Paper appointment book
Computer or online system

Cheap; needs only the book and a pencil

Seeing free times
The whole day at a glance, but one page in one place

Written in **pencil** so that moves and cancellations can be rubbed out neatly

Not possible
**Online booking** on the salon's website or app at any hour; staff must still check new bookings and keep the system up to date

blocks.note: A salon that uses a computer system still prints or writes out a **day list** each morning. If the power or the internet fails, as it can anywhere in Jamaica, the day goes on from the list.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: To save space, many salons write short codes in the book: 'C/B' for cut and blow-dry, 'R/T' for a relaxer touch-up, 'MP' for a manicure and pedicure, 'ST' for a skin test. Codes only work when **every** member of staff knows them, so the salon keeps a list of its codes by the book and does not let people invent their own.

The appointment book and the booking screen hold clients' names, numbers and services. Keep the book closed and the screen turned away from clients at the desk, do not read other clients' bookings out loud while you look for a free time, and lock the screen when you leave the desk.

head: Detail
Why
rows: The client's **full name**
To find her record, and to tell two Miss Browns apart.
Her **phone number**
To confirm, remind, or reach her if the worker is sick or the salon must close.
The **service** (or services)
Decides the time, the price and the worker.
The **worker**
Her usual stylist, or one trained for the service and free.
The **date and time**
Written in the right column and across the right rows.
**Special needs or notes**
A first visit, a skin test needed, pregnancy, a disability, an allergy, a child, 'wants to discuss colour'.
The **price**, any **deposit** and the **cancellation policy**
So that there are no surprises at check-out and the rules are fair.

blocks.h: The booking call, step by step

flow: Answer with the salon's name and yours
Ask for a preferred worker; check skills
Find a slot long enough; offer two or three
Check for tests or consultation needed
Write it in; read it all back

ul: If the client does not know what she needs, for example for damaged hair, do not guess a service over the phone. Book a **consultation** with a stylist first, or a consultation at the start of a longer slot.
A worker is booked only for services she is **trained** to do. A client who asks for acrylic nails is booked with a nail technician trained in acrylics, not with whoever is free.
Offer **two or three** choices of time rather than asking 'When do you want to come?': it is quicker, and it steers the client to the gaps you need to fill.

When she says she is pregnant, has a medical condition, or wants a service you are not sure is suitable (a massage in pregnancy, a chemical service on a sore scalp), **note it and ask the therapist or stylist** before confirming. The decision is theirs.
**Read every detail back**: name, service, worker, date, time, price. Most booking mistakes are caught here.
Give her an **appointment card** if she books at the desk, with the date, time, service and worker on it.

Check the online booking system several times a day. A client who books online at midnight expects her slot to be there in the morning. Make sure online slots match the real book, and that a worker's day off is blocked out online too.

A **walk-in** is a client with no appointment. Check the book for a worker who is trained for the service and free for the full time. If the salon is fully booked, apologise and offer the **next free time** or another day; take her name and number. Do not squeeze her into a slot that is too short, and do not push a booked client back for her.

blocks.note: Reminders and confirmations are sent only to clients who have **agreed** to receive them, and only to the number or e-mail they gave. A reminder the day before, by text message (SMS) or a call, cuts down no-shows and gives the client a chance to change the booking in time.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Service times and planning the day

blocks.p: Every service takes a set time, and the salon keeps a **list of service times** by the book. The receptionist must know them, or look them up, for every booking. Too little time booked, and the worker runs late, every later client waits, and the worker rushes and makes mistakes. Too much time booked, and the chair sits empty and the salon loses money.

ul: The **consultation** at the start.
The work itself, including the shampoo.

**Processing time** for chemical services: the time a relaxer, colour, perm or tint is left on the hair to work. During a long processing time, some salons let the worker start a short service for another client, if it is safe and the first client is checked on; follow the salon's rule.
**Clean-up and set-up** of the station between clients.
Where the worker is also the receptionist, time to check clients out.

blocks.p: Add the hours first, then the minutes. If the minutes come to 60 or more, take away 60 and add one to the hours. To find how many services fit in a period, change everything to minutes and divide. Work every sum twice.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: A wash and set takes 1 hour 15 minutes and starts at 2:35 p.m. When does it end?
A relaxer touch-up (1 hour 45 minutes) is followed by a trim (30 minutes) with the same stylist from 9:50 a.m. When is she free?
1 h 45 + 30 min = 2 h 15 min. 9:50 + 2 hours = 11:50; 50 + 15 = 65 minutes = 1 hour 5 minutes
How many 50-minute massages can a therapist do between 10:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. with no breaks?
3 hours = 180 minutes; 180 ÷ 50 = 3.6
3 full massages (with 30 minutes over)
A client arrives at 3:25 p.m. for a 3:00 p.m. booking. How late is she?
25 minutes
How many minutes are 1 and three-quarter hours?
105 minutes

ul: Block out breaks, lunch, days off, training and any set finish time before you book anything else.
Book the full service time, and the clean-up time the salon allows.
Put long services where they fit the worker's energy and the salon's rush, as the supervisor advises; put a short service in a short gap rather than leaving it empty.
Leave a little **slack** on a busy day for walk-ins, late arrivals and a service that runs over.
**Check the column before every booking**, however sure you are that it is free. **Double booking** (two clients with one worker at the same time) comes from not looking.

blocks.p: A **standing appointment** is a booking kept for the same client at the same day and time at regular intervals, for example every second Friday at 10:00 a.m. for a wash and set. Standing appointments are written into the book ahead for weeks or months, and they are the backbone of a stylist's column. Confirm them as you would any booking.

When a client rebooks 'in four weeks', count the weeks from the date of her visit: four weeks after Monday 2 March is Monday 30 March. Six weeks after 10 September is 22 October. Say the date and the day together, and check it against a calendar.

sections.title: Skin tests, consultations and chemical services

blocks.p: Chemical services, such as hair colour, lighteners, relaxers and perms, and tints for lashes and brows, can cause an allergic reaction or damage the hair, skin or scalp. Booking them needs more care than booking a wash and set.

ul: Many manufacturers require a **skin (patch) test** before a colour or tint, often **48 hours** before the service, and sometimes before every service or again after a gap or a change of product. The receptionist does not decide whether a test is needed: she **checks the client's record** and asks the stylist or therapist.

The test is booked **early enough**. For a lash tint on Saturday morning that needs a test 48 hours before, the test must be done by Thursday morning at the latest, so you book it on Thursday or earlier.
The test is a short desk or chair appointment, written in the book like any other.

The **result** is written on the client's record with the date, so that every member of staff can see that it was done, when, and that it was clear. The service goes ahead only if the test was negative.
A client who arrives for a colour with no test recorded is **not** sent through for the colour. The stylist is told, and the stylist decides what can be done.

blocks.p: A new client, a client with damaged hair or a scalp problem, or a client who wants a big change may need a **consultation** before the service is booked, so that the stylist can look at the hair and scalp and plan the right service and time. A consultation may be a short separate appointment or the first part of a longer slot. If the stylist finds a reason the service cannot go ahead, it is not booked, and the client may be advised to see a doctor.

flow: Client asks for colour or a chemical service
Book the skin test early enough
Book the service with a trained worker
Allow the full time, with processing
Remind the client of the test

blocks.note: Never let a client talk you into skipping a test 'because she has had the colour before'. Allergies can start at any time. The rule protects her and the salon.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A booked hour that goes unused cannot be sold again: the worker was paid to be there and the chair stood empty. Late arrivals push every later client back. Salons protect themselves with **policies** on notice for cancellations, late arrivals, no-shows and deposits. A policy is only fair if the client is **told when she books**, so the receptionist explains it every time, and it is printed on the appointment card or the website.

head: Situation
What you do
rows: A client phones to **cancel**
Thank her for letting you know
Remove the booking (rub it out, or cancel it on the system) so that the time shows as free
Offer her a new time
If the salon keeps a **waiting list**, call the next client on it and offer the free slot
A client wants to **move (reschedule)** her booking
Find a new slot with the same worker, or another suitable one
Move the booking; make sure the old slot is cleared
Read back the new date and time
A client is **late**
Greet her politely; do not scold
Work out how late she is and how much of her slot is left
Check with the worker what can be done in the time
Offer a shorter service, the next free time, or a new booking
Do not make the next client wait
A client is a **no-show** (misses her booking without telling the salon)
Try to contact her
Mark the no-show on her record
Apply the salon's policy: a deposit may be kept or a fee charged, as the policy says
Offer the time to a walk-in or the waiting list
A **worker is off sick**
Look at her column for the day
**Call each client** as early as possible: explain, apologise, and offer another worker with the right skills or a new time
Note who has been reached and who has not; keep trying
Tell the supervisor
The salon must **close** (a hurricane warning, a power failure, a water lock-off)
Call every booked client
Rebook as soon as the salon can reopen

ul: A **deposit** is part of the price paid at the time of booking. Salons ask for one for **long or costly bookings**, such as a bridal party, a spa day, a full head of braids or extensions, or for a client who has not turned up before. The deposit is taken off the bill on the day. If the client cancels late or does not come, the deposit may be kept, as the policy says.
A **cancellation fee** may be charged when a booking is cancelled with less than the notice the policy requires (often 24 hours).
Give a **receipt** for every deposit, and record it on the booking and the client's record, so that it is not forgotten or charged twice at check-out.

blocks.p: A bride and four bridesmaids, a birthday spa day for four friends, a dance troupe before a show: group bookings need planning with the staff, not just a line in the book. Take the organiser's name and number and the date. List who needs which services. Check which workers are trained and free, and **draw up a timetable** that moves the guests between workers and rooms so that nobody is double booked and everyone finishes on time. Book lunch or breaks where the whole group is free. Ask about allergies, medical conditions and pregnancy. Quote the package price, take a **deposit** and explain the cancellation policy. Send the timetable to the organiser in writing, remind her a few days before, and tell the staff so that they can prepare.

sections.title: Checking out: the bill and the payment

blocks.p: Check-out is the last thing a client remembers. It should be quick, accurate and warm. It is also the salon's best chance to find out whether she is happy, to put a problem right before she leaves, and to book her next visit.

flow: Greet her by name; ask how it went
If she has a concern, deal with it first
Check the service ticket against the booking
Prepare the bill; explain each line
Take payment; give change or slip and a receipt
Help with belongings; thank her; invite her back

blocks.p: Ask how her service went and look at the result. The visit is fresh in her mind, so this is the moment to hear feedback, and a problem spotted now can be fixed before she goes. If she is not happy, **listen, apologise that she is unhappy, and call the stylist or supervisor** before you take any money. Do not argue, and do not decide on a discount or refund yourself.

The **service ticket** (or the stylist's note on the system) lists what was actually done and the products used or sold. Check it against the booking: a client booked for a cut may have added a treatment, or decided against the blow-dry. Billing from the booking alone gets the bill wrong. If the ticket is unclear, ask the stylist, not the client.

ol: List every **service** she had, with its price from the current price list.
Add any **product** she is buying, with its price.

Check any **voucher or discount**: the salon's own, in date, not already used, and what it covers (for example, 10% off services only, not products). Work out the discount on the right items and take it off.
Add **GCT** at the current rate, as the till or the price list shows. Some salons' prices already include GCT; others add it at the till. Know which your salon does, and say so on the bill.
Take off any **deposit** paid at booking, after checking the deposit record or receipt.
Check the sums again, or let the till work them out and check the till.
**Explain each line** to the client before she pays: each item, its price, the discount, the GCT and the total.

head: Item
J$
rows: Relaxer touch-up (service)
Trim (service)
Services total
Discount voucher: 10% off services only (10% of 8,000)
Services after discount
Leave-in conditioner (product)
Total before GCT
GCT at the current rate
added as the till shows
Deposit paid at booking
Amount to pay
total with GCT, less 2,000

blocks.p: Notice that the voucher is applied **only to the services**, not to the product, and that the deposit comes off at the end, after GCT has been added, because the client already paid that part.

head: Question
Working
Answer
rows: Pedicure J$3,200 and manicure J$2,500; nail polish J$1,100. Total before tax?
A 15% voucher on services of J$6,000. Discount?
Bridal package J$45,000; deposit paid J$15,000. Left to pay?
Bill J$7,350; client gives J$10,000 cash. Change?

blocks.note: GCT (General Consumption Tax) is added 'at the current rate'. The rate can change, so never quote a figure from memory: use the rate the till, the price list or the assessor gives.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Cash: count it in front of her, say the amount, put it in the till, count the change back into her hand and give a receipt.
Card: follow the machine's steps; let her enter her PIN privately; give her the customer slip and the receipt. Never write down card numbers.
Mobile or bank transfer, where the salon accepts it: check that the payment has arrived before she leaves.
Vouchers, gift certificates and loyalty cards: check they are valid and record their use.

A client who **cannot pay the full bill** today: stay polite, do not argue at the desk, and **call the supervisor**, who follows the salon's policy. Do not decide yourself to let her owe money, and do not embarrass her in front of others.
Keep the till closed between sales. Count it as the salon's procedure says.

sections.title: Rebooking, aftercare, home care and records

blocks.p: Offer the next appointment **before she leaves**. It keeps her look on track, and it fills the worker's column weeks ahead. Link the offer to what the stylist advised: 'Marcia suggests a touch-up in about six to eight weeks. Shall I book that now?' The right gap depends on the service and the stylist's advice.

head: Service
Typical gap before the next visit (the stylist advises)
rows: Relaxer touch-up
Often 6 to 10 weeks, when the new growth shows
Permanent colour regrowth
Often 4 to 6 weeks
Cut and shape
Often 4 to 8 weeks
Gel or acrylic nails
Fill or refill often every 2 to 3 weeks
Braids, twists, weave
As the stylist advises; often 6 to 8 weeks before take-down
Facial
Often every 4 weeks

blocks.p: Write the rebooking in the book and give her an **appointment card** with the date, time, service and worker. Offer a reminder if she agrees to receive them.

Aftercare is the advice that helps the client keep the result and avoid problems at home: when she may wash after a relaxer, how to sleep on a set, how to care for nails, what to avoid after a facial. The stylist gives it at the chair; the receptionist makes sure the client **has** it, often as a printed **aftercare leaflet**, and answers simple questions or refers harder ones back to the stylist.
The products the stylist used and recommends are often on the retail shelf. Selling them is part of good service, not pushiness, when it is done honestly.

ul: Link the product to the stylist's advice: 'Your stylist used this leave-in; it is what she recommends for keeping the moisture in.'
Show her the product, explain what it does and tell her the **price**. Offer a tester.
Accept a 'no' politely, give her a leaflet or the price list, and invite her to ask next time.
Never add a product to the bill that she has not agreed to buy, and never claim a product does something it does not.

head: Record after the visit
Example
rows: Date, services, worker
12 June; relaxer touch-up and trim; Marcia
Products used, strength or shade, processing time, result
Regular-strength relaxer, 18 minutes; even result
Tests, reactions, allergies, contra-indications
Skin test 10 June negative; no reaction
Products bought
Leave-in conditioner
Next booking
24 July, 10:00 a.m., Marcia
Comments, preferences, complaints and how they were solved
Prefers a front-wash basin
Phone number checked
Yes

ul: Paper records in a closed file or a locked drawer; computer records behind a **password**, with the screen locked when the desk is left.
Never read out or show one client's details to another; never share or sell them.
Jamaica's **data protection law** requires businesses to keep personal information safe and to use it only for the purpose it was given.

blocks.p: Thank her **by name**, help her with her belongings and the door, and invite her back: 'Thank you, Mrs. Campbell. We'll see you on the 24th.' The last thirty seconds of a visit are the ones she carries home.

ul: I can explain what an appointment system is for and how a day page is laid out.
I can compare a paper book with a computer or online system and say why a backup is kept.
I can take a booking with every detail needed and read it back.
I can book a worker who is trained for the service, for the full time, including processing time.
I can work out when a service ends, how many fit in a period, how late a client is and the date of a rebooking.
I can explain processing time, standing appointments, free slots, walk-ins and double booking.
I can book a skin test early enough before a colour or tint and say why the result is recorded.
I can say when a consultation should be booked first.
I can deal with a cancellation, a moved booking, a late client, a no-show and a worker off sick.
I can explain deposits, cancellation fees and why policies are explained at booking.
I can plan a group booking.
I can check a client out: check she is happy, check the ticket, prepare and explain the bill.
I can apply a discount to the right items, add GCT at the given rate and take off a deposit.
I can add up a bill, work out a percentage discount and give correct change.
I can take cash and card payments and give a receipt, and call the supervisor when a client cannot pay.
I can offer rebooking, an appointment card, aftercare advice and home-care products without pushing.
I can update a client's record and keep it private.
I can say goodbye in a way that brings the client back.

blocks.note: In the exam, show your working for time and money sums and check them twice. Write times with a.m. or p.m. and money with J$.
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: Monday's phone calls in Mandeville
c1.text: Nickeisha is the receptionist at a hair and nail salon in Mandeville. The salon's service times are: relaxer touch-up 1 hour 45 minutes; wash and set 1 hour 15 minutes; gel nails 1 hour; brow tint 20 minutes (skin test needed 48 hours before, as the maker says). The stylist Petal is trained in relaxers and sets; the nail technician Georgia does gel nails only; the therapist Mona does brow tints and facials. On Monday morning Nickeisha takes a call from Miss Tamara Blake, who wants a relaxer touch-up followed by a wash and set with Petal, starting at 1:15 p.m. on Wednesday, and a brow tint 'while she is there'. Tamara has never had a brow tint at the salon.

c2.title: A bridal party for Lucea
c2.text: Mrs. Donna Campbell phones a salon in Lucea to book hair and make-up for herself and three bridesmaids on Saturday 27 June, for a 3:00 p.m. wedding. Each person needs hair (1 hour 30 minutes) and make-up (45 minutes). The salon has two stylists and one make-up artist on that day. Mrs. Campbell asks whether she can 'just confirm on the Friday before'. The salon's policy is a 30% deposit on group bookings and 48 hours' notice to cancel. The package price is J$60,000.

c3.title: A day that comes apart in Ocho Rios
c3.text: On Thursday at 8:10 a.m. the stylist Shernette calls a salon in Ocho Rios to say she is sick. Her column shows a 9:00 a.m. wash and set, a 10:30 a.m. relaxer touch-up, a 1:00 p.m. cut and blow-dry and a 2:30 p.m. wash and set. The other stylist, Carlene, is trained in all of these and has free slots at 10:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. At 9:40 a.m. a walk-in asks for a wash and set 'right now'. The salon has a paper appointment book kept in pencil and a waiting list with two names for Thursday.

c4.title: Check-out at a spa in Runaway Bay
c4.text: Mrs. Janet Reid is checking out of a spa in Runaway Bay. Her service ticket shows a facial (J$8,000) and a back massage (J$7,000); her booking also listed a pedicure, which the therapist's ticket says she decided not to have. She is buying a moisturiser (J$3,500). She has a voucher for 10% off services only, and she paid a J$5,000 deposit when she booked. The assessor's GCT rate for the exercise is 15%. Trainee Jerome is at the desk.

c5.title: Not quite happy in Santa Cruz
c5.text: Miss Kerry-Ann Brown comes to the desk of a salon in Santa Cruz after a cut and colour with the stylist Delroy. She says the cut is lovely but the colour is 'a bit more red than I expected'. Delroy is already shampooing his next client. The supervisor, Mrs. Palmer, is in the salon. Kerry-Ann is also asking when she should come back and what she should use at home, and she says she does not want 'to be sold a whole shelf of products'.

questions.q: If Tamara's relaxer touch-up and wash and set with Petal start at 1:15 p.m. on Wednesday, when will Petal be free?
questions.why: 1 hour 45 minutes plus 1 hour 15 minutes is 3 hours. 1:15 p.m. plus 3 hours is 4:15 p.m.

questions.q: Can Nickeisha book the brow tint for Wednesday as well?
o: Yes, with Petal straight after the set, as the tint takes only 20 minutes
Yes, with Mona, as a first tint needs no test if she has no allergies
Only if she has a skin test by Monday afternoon and it is clear
No, a tint can never be done on the same day as a chemical hair service
questions.why: The maker requires a skin test 48 hours before a tint. For a Wednesday afternoon tint, the test must be done by Monday afternoon, and the tint is booked with Mona, who is trained for it; Petal is not.

questions.q: Tamara wants gel nails too and asks for Petal to do them 'since she is doing everything else'. What should Nickeisha say?
o: That Petal can do them if she is free, as stylists can apply gel nails
That gel nails cannot be booked on the same day as a relaxer touch-up
That Tamara should ask Petal herself on Wednesday whether she will do them
That gel nails are done by Georgia, and offer a time with her
questions.why: A worker is booked only for services she is trained to do. Georgia does gel nails; Petal does hair. The receptionist offers a suitable time with the right worker.

questions.q: Before ending the call, what is the most important thing Nickeisha must do?
o: Read the bookings back to Tamara: services, workers, times and prices
Ask Tamara to call back on Tuesday to confirm that she is still coming
Tell Tamara which products Petal will use for the relaxer touch-up
Write Tamara's bookings on a note to copy into the book later
questions.why: Reading back every detail is how most booking mistakes are caught. Bookings are written straight into the book, and a reminder is the salon's job, not the client's.

questions.q: Which plan allows each of the four women to have her hair and make-up done, with the salon's staff, in good time for a 3:00 p.m. wedding?
o: Book all four for hair at 11:00 a.m. and all four for make-up at 12:30 p.m.
A written timetable rotating the four between the staff, starting early enough
Book the bride only, as the bridesmaids can be fitted in as walk-ins on the day
Book the two stylists to do hair and make-up for two women each, so the make-up artist is free
questions.why: A group booking needs a timetable planned with the staff, so that no worker or room is double booked and everyone finishes on time. Four women cannot have hair at once with two stylists, and bridesmaids are not left to chance.

questions.q: How much deposit should Nickeisha's colleague in Lucea take, and how much will Mrs. Campbell owe on the day?
o: J$30,000 deposit; J$30,000 on the day
J$18,000 deposit; J$60,000 on the day
J$6,000 deposit; J$54,000 on the day
J$18,000 deposit; J$42,000 on the day
questions.why: 30% of J$60,000 is 60,000 × 30 ÷ 100 = J$18,000. The deposit is taken off the price, so 60,000 − 18,000 = J$42,000 remains (plus GCT as the salon's price list shows).

questions.q: Mrs. Campbell wants to 'just confirm on the Friday before'. What should the receptionist tell her?
o: That the policy needs 48 hours' notice, so changes must be made by Thursday
That the Friday is fine, as a bridal party is too valuable to refuse
That she must confirm by Monday that week or the booking will be given away
That no confirmation is needed, because the deposit has been paid already
questions.why: The cancellation policy is explained at booking so that it is fair. With 48 hours' notice for a Saturday afternoon booking, the last day to change it is Thursday afternoon, and the deposit may be kept if the policy is broken.

questions.q: What should the receptionist in Ocho Rios do first after Shernette's call?
o: Wait to see whether the 9:00 a.m. client arrives, then explain to her in person
Rub out all four bookings so that the column is free for walk-ins
Move all four bookings into Carlene's column without calling anyone
Phone her 9:00 a.m. client first, then the rest, offering Carlene or a new time
questions.why: Clients are called as early as possible, the earliest booking first, and offered another trained worker or a new time. Nobody should travel in to find her stylist absent, and nobody is moved to another stylist without being asked.

questions.q: Which of Shernette's clients can be offered Carlene at their booked times?
o: The 9:00 a.m. wash and set and the 1:00 p.m. cut and blow-dry
All four, because Carlene is trained in every one of the services
The 10:30 a.m. relaxer touch-up and the 2:30 p.m. wash and set
None, because a client may only be moved to her own stylist's slot
questions.why: Carlene is free at 10:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m., so those two clients can be offered her at their own times. The 9:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. clients need new times or another day.

questions.q: The walk-in at 9:40 a.m. wants a wash and set now. Carlene's 10:30 a.m. slot has just been taken by the moved relaxer client. What should the receptionist do?
o: Start her with Carlene now and let the relaxer client wait a little when she arrives
Apologise and offer the next free time or another day, taking her name and number
Book her into Shernette's empty 9:00 a.m. slot, as Shernette is off anyway
Ask Carlene to do a quicker set in the 50 minutes before her 10:30 a.m. client
questions.why: A walk-in is given a slot long enough for the full service with a trained worker who is free. Shernette is absent, so her slot is not a real one, and a booked client is not pushed back or a service squeezed.

questions.q: A cancellation for 1:00 p.m. with Carlene comes in at 10:00 a.m. What should happen to the slot?
o: Leave it written in, in case the client changes her mind and comes
Give it to the first of Carlene's afternoon clients so that she finishes early
Clear it in the book and offer it to the names on the waiting list
Write 'cancelled' in ink over the booking so that nobody uses the slot
questions.why: A cancelled booking is removed so the time shows as free, and the waiting list is called first. Pencil is used so that the slot can be rubbed out cleanly and rebooked.

questions.q: Which services should Jerome put on Mrs. Reid's bill?
o: The facial, the back massage and the pedicure
The facial only, as the massage was not booked
The facial and the back massage only
The pedicure and the facial, as booked
questions.why: The bill is made from the service ticket, which shows what was actually done, checked against the booking. The pedicure was booked but not done, so it is not charged.

questions.q: What is the discount from Mrs. Reid's voucher?
questions.why: The voucher is 10% off services only. Services are 8,000 + 7,000 = J$15,000, and 10% of 15,000 is J$1,500. The moisturiser is not discounted.

questions.q: Using the assessor's rate of 15%, what is Mrs. Reid's total before the deposit is taken off?
After the deposit, how much does Mrs. Reid pay today, and what must Jerome do before he takes it?
o: J$19,550; ask her whether she remembers paying a deposit when booking
J$14,550; take her card quickly so the next client is not kept waiting long
J$12,000; take the deposit off the services before adding the product on
J$14,550; check the deposit record and explain each bill line
questions.why: 19,550 − 5,000 = J$14,550. The deposit is checked against its record and taken off after GCT, and every line is explained before the client pays.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann says the colour is more red than she expected. What should the receptionist do first?
o: Listen to her, apologise, and fetch Mrs. Palmer before taking any payment
Explain that red tones always look stronger on freshly washed hair, and will settle in
Take payment for the cut now and tell her to come back if the colour still worries her later
Offer 10% off the colour so that she leaves satisfied and the next client can be served quickly
questions.why: A concern is dealt with before the bill. The receptionist listens and apologises for her experience, then brings the supervisor or the stylist; discounts and explanations about the result are not hers to give.

questions.q: Delroy has advised a trim and colour refresh in six weeks. Which is the best way to offer the rebooking?
o: 'Delroy suggests about six weeks. Shall I book that for you now, with him?'
'Most clients book monthly, so I will put you down for the same time next month, then.'
'Call us when you notice the roots; we are usually able to fit people in at short notice.'
'You need to book today or you may not get Delroy again for several months.'
questions.why: Rebooking is linked to the stylist's advice and offered as a choice. It is not imposed, left to chance, or used to pressure the client.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann does not want 'a whole shelf of products'. How should the receptionist handle home care?
o: Add the recommended shampoo to the bill, as the stylist's advice counts as her agreement
Mention the product Delroy recommended, its use and price, and accept her answer
Say nothing about products, since she has made it clear she will not buy any at all
Offer a discount on three products if she buys them all together today
questions.why: Honest, helpful advice linked to what the stylist recommended builds trust; a 'no' is accepted politely. Nothing is added to a bill without agreement, and pressure drives clients away.

questions.q: After Kerry-Ann leaves, what should be added to her record?
o: Only her next booking, as the colour details are in the stylist's notes
The services and shade, her comment on the red tone, and her next booking
The amount she paid and the receptionist's opinion of her as a client
Nothing today, since the complaint record already holds the colour comment
questions.why: The record carries the services, products and shades, any comment or complaint and how it was solved, and the next booking, so that the next visit can be planned and the colour adjusted.

questions.q: A client books a facial every four weeks. Her last visit was Tuesday 5 May. What is the date of her next standing appointment?
o: Tuesday 26 May
Tuesday 9 June
Friday 5 June
Tuesday 2 June
questions.why: Four weeks is 28 days. May has 31 days, so 5 May + 28 days = 33 May = 2 June, and it falls on the same weekday, a Tuesday.
